content:
The [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Calculate the determinant, trace and transpose of a 2 × 2 or 3 × 3 matrix. Enter your matrix size and matrix values by row and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

A determinant is a scalar calculated from a square matrix. It encodes whether the matrix is invertible and how its linear transformation scales area in two dimensions or volume in three. This calculator evaluates 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 real matrices, shows the trace and transpose, and identifies singular matrices whose determinant is zero. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Matrix Determinant Calculator

Start by choosing your matrix size from the list, then typing or pasting your matrix values by row. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Choose 2 × 2 or 3 × 3 and enter exactly four or nine numeric coefficients.
2. Arrange entries row by row, using commas or whitespace between values and line breaks between rows.
3. Read the determinant and invertibility result; the transpose and trace provide useful checks for further matrix work.

## Formula

2 × 2: |A| = ad − bc. 3 × 3 uses cofactor expansion: a(ei−fh) − b(di−fg) + c(dh−eg). Trace = sum of diagonal entries.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. For [[2,1,3],[4,0,5],[1,−2,2]], the determinant is −7 and the trace is 4. Because the determinant is non-zero, the matrix is invertible. Try the same figures in the [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Matrix size: 3 × 3, Matrix values by row: 2, 1, 3 4, 0, 5 1, -2, 2), the [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) returns Determinant: -7, Matrix type: Non-singular — invertible, Trace: 4, Transpose: 2, 4, 1 1, 0, -2 3, 5, 2. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## What a zero determinant means

A zero determinant means the rows or columns are linearly dependent. The transformation collapses space onto a lower dimension, so it cannot be reversed by a unique inverse matrix. A non-zero determinant establishes invertibility, although a determinant very close to zero can indicate numerical ill-conditioning.

## Determinants, area and volume

For a 2 × 2 matrix, the absolute determinant is the area of the parallelogram formed by its column vectors. For 3 × 3 it is the volume scale factor of the corresponding parallelepiped. The sign reflects orientation: swapping two rows reverses the sign without changing the absolute scale factor.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Keep row order consistent; swapping rows changes the determinant's sign.
- Use decimal points rather than decimal commas as separators.
- Near-zero floating-point results are treated as singular only within a very small numerical tolerance.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a non-square matrix have a determinant?

No. The determinant is defined only for square matrices. This page supports the common 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 cases. Try it with your own numbers in the [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does determinant zero mean every entry is zero?

No. Many non-zero matrices are singular. For example, two identical rows make the determinant zero even when all entries are non-zero. Try it with your own numbers in the [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the trace?

The trace is the sum of entries on the main diagonal, from top left to bottom right. It is not generally the same as the determinant. Try it with your own numbers in the [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Matrix Determinant Calculator use?

2 × 2: |A| = ad − bc. 3 × 3 uses cofactor expansion: a(ei−fh) − b(di−fg) + c(dh−eg). Trace = sum of diagonal entries. You can see it in action in the [Matrix Determinant Calculator](/matrix-determinant-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
